strengths: Well-motivated problem: Trajectory-conditioned video generation frequently suffers from visual distortion and feature entanglement during physical contact/overlap between robotic grippers and manipulated objects.

Intuitive collaborative trajectory formulation: Decomposing the manipulation timeline into pre-interaction, interaction, and post-interaction phases with dominant and submissive subject latents effectively avoids feature ambiguity in overlapping regions.
Comprehensive experimental setup: All baselines (Tora, DragAnything, MotionCtrl, IRASim) are retrained on CogVideoX-5B on the Bridge V2 dataset under consistent settings, ensuring a fair comparison.

Extensive ablations: The ablations thoroughly examine the impact of causal embeddings, mask representations versus point tracks, separate versus collaborative trajectory schemes, and robustness to trajectory perturbation and mask sparsity.
weaknesses: Inference/Annotation constraints: While the paper argues that the framework simplifies user input compared to drawing two full-length trajectories, requiring the user to explicitly specify interaction temporal boundaries (start and end frames $F_1, F_2$) still imposes a non-trivial annotation overhead and potential trial-and-error.

Assumption on interaction dynamics: The dominant/submissive decomposition assumes a single primary object manipulated by a single gripper. It remains unclear how the formulation extends cleanly to tool-use, multi-object chain reactions, or tasks where both objects move simultaneously (e.g., pouring from a moving cup into a moving bowl).

Missing downstream policy evaluation: Despite framing the motivation around generating data for robot decision-making and world models, the paper solely measures standard video synthesis and trajectory tracking metrics without evaluating downstream robotic policy learning (e.g., BC/diffusion policy training success rate).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: Tackling feature entanglement and visual degradation during physical contact/overlap in trajectory-guided video generation is an important and practical problem for robotic manipulation simulation.

Effective collaborative trajectory design: Decomposing manipulation into pre-interaction, interaction, and post-interaction stages cleanly avoids the conflicting feature fusion issues seen in prior separate multi-trajectory baselines.

Rigorous and fair baseline comparison: The authors retrained strong baselines (Tora, DragAnything, MotionCtrl, IRASim) on the same CogVideoX-5B backbone and curated Bridge V2 data, ensuring a fair and credible benchmark comparison.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation and ablations: The empirical validation covers visual quality (FVD, PSNR, SSIM, VBench), trajectory-following accuracy, user studies, and thorough component-level ablations (e.g., causal latents, mask vs. point representations, mask sparsity, trajectory perturbation).
Practical user interaction considerations: Demonstrating robustness to coarse brush strokes and sparse annotations significantly enhances user-friendliness for interactive simulation workflows.
weaknesses: Lack of downstream policy evaluation: While the paper heavily motivates itself as a world simulator for robot learning and data synthesis, it does not evaluate whether policies trained on the generated videos achieve higher task success rates or bridge sim-to-real gaps.

Evaluation scope primarily limited to Bridge V2: Quantitative evaluations are restricted to Bridge V2 data. Testing on other robot manipulation benchmarks (e.g., RH20T, CALVIN, or Open X-Embodiment subsets) would have strengthened claims of generalizability across diverse robot embodiments and setups.

Reliance on 2D image-space trajectory control: The trajectory formulation operates purely in 2D image coordinates, which can struggle with significant camera perspective changes or complex 3D depth-dependent interactions (e.g., reaching into containers or occluded insertions).

Manual temporal phase specification at test time: Generating videos requires specifying transition boundaries (start/end frames of the interaction phase), which adds user overhead compared to end-to-end goal-directed trajectory conditioning.

strengths: Well-motivated formulation: Decomposing the manipulation timeline into pre-interaction, interaction, and post-interaction phases and alternating the driving entity (manipulator vs. manipulated object) provides a neat inductive bias that directly mitigates multi-object feature entanglement in trajectory-controlled video generation.

Fair and rigorous baseline comparison: The authors retrained all competitive baselines (Tora, DragAnything, MotionCtrl, IRASim) on the exact same backbone (CogVideoX-5B) and curated dataset, ensuring an apple-to-apple comparison.

Comprehensive experimental validation: The quantitative evaluation spans visual fidelity (FVD, PSNR, SSIM), trajectory tracking errors (robot and object), standard VBench dimensions, and a user preference study, showing consistent improvements across the board.

Informative ablation studies: The ablations thoroughly examine causal visual embeddings, mask vs. point representations, collaborative vs. separate trajectories, motion injection mechanisms, mask sparsity robustness, and trajectory perturbations.
weaknesses: No downstream policy evaluation: While the paper frames the method as an interactive simulator for generating robotic decision-making data, the generated videos are assessed purely via perceptual and trajectory tracking metrics. Validating whether policies trained on these generated videos transfer to robot control (either in sim or real) would significantly elevate the paper's impact.

Requirement of temporal phase segmentation: The collaborative formulation requires knowing or annotating the interaction boundary frames (F1 and F2). While automated via heuristics during dataset curation, human users must manually specify these timestamps at test time, introducing non-negligible user overhead.

Limitation to 2D trajectory space: Control is defined exclusively via 2D screen-space pixel trajectories. For complex 3D manipulations with depth variations, out-of-plane rotations, or severe perspective foreshortening, 2D coordinates lack 3D spatial awareness, which can limit physical plausibility.

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation: The paper clearly identifies a major pain point in existing trajectory-controlled video generation methods (e.g., Tora, DragAnything)—feature entanglement and visual degradation when independently conditioning multiple overlapping trajectories during physical interaction.

Intuitive and elegant technical design: Decomposing the manipulation into pre-interaction, interaction, and post-interaction phases and alternating the conditioning focus between the dominant agent (gripper) and the submissive agent (object) is physically intuitive and avoids overlapping trajectory conflicts.

Comprehensive evaluation across vision and robotics: The method is validated not only using conventional video generation metrics (FVD, PSNR, SSIM, TrajError, and VBench) on the Bridge dataset, but also on downstream robotic action planning tasks in RLBench and SIMPLER via inverse dynamics extraction.

Solid ablations and robustness analyses: The authors provide detailed ablation experiments studying the causal representation, mask vs. point representations, mask sparsity, trajectory perturbation, and sensitivity to inaccurate prompts.
weaknesses: Requirement for temporal interaction boundaries: At test/inference time, the framework expects users to specify the interaction start and end frames ($F_1, F_2$) or rely on heuristic/coarse interval boundaries, which adds friction to fully automated test-time deployment.

2D control constraint: The model operates purely with 2D image-space trajectories rather than 3D/6-DoF end-effector poses, which limits its ability to model complex out-of-plane rotations and depth variations in robotic manipulation.

Minor notation and typographical errors: Equation (6) contains inconsistent subscript indexing ($\hat{\epsilon}_{	heta 1}$), and Table 7 has a typo in the column header ('Deviration' instead of 'Deviation').

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation: The paper clearly identifies and tackles the feature entanglement issue that occurs in prior trajectory-conditioned video diffusion models when multiple trajectories overlap during physical robot-object interactions.

Intuitive and structured interaction decomposition: Partitioning manipulation trajectories temporally into pre-interaction, interaction, and post-interaction stages allows the model to dynamically alternate the driving agent (robot arm vs. manipulated object), effectively avoiding conflicting multi-trajectory feature guidance.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: The authors evaluate across standard video fidelity metrics (FVD, PSNR, SSIM, VBench), trajectory tracking accuracy, user studies, and downstream robotic policy execution on both RLBench and SIMPLER via inverse dynamics modeling.

Thorough ablation studies: The paper systematically validates individual components, including the causal latent propagation, mask vs. point representations, sensitivity to trajectory perturbations, mask sparsity, and prompt noise.
weaknesses: Heuristic shape representation: The shape-aware embedding approximates the object's spatial extent as a uniform circular volume with radius proportional to mask area. This isotropic simplification struggles to accurately capture elongated, articulated, or asymmetrical objects (e.g., knives, open box flaps, tools), which are common in manipulation.

Reliance on manual interaction segmentation and annotation: While presented as user-friendly, specifying the temporal boundaries (start/end of interaction) and spatial trajectories adds annotation overhead. Furthermore, as shown in Table R11, automated segmentation tools like Grounded-SAM exhibit high failure rates in multi-object scenes, necessitating substantial manual filtering and correction.
Lack of 3D physical grounding: Operating purely in 2D image space limits the method's ability to handle out-of-plane rotations, occlusions, and depth variations inherent to 3D physical manipulation.

Evaluation restricted to simulation: Downstream embodied action planning is only verified on simulated benchmarks (RLBench and SIMPLER) using inverse dynamics; evaluation on physical robotic hardware under real-world sensing and contact uncertainties is missing.

strengths: Well-motivated approach: Decomposing manipulation into pre-interaction, interaction, and post-interaction stages smartly circumvents the feature entanglement and occlusion ambiguities that plague independent multi-trajectory conditioning methods (like Tora and DragAnything).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The proposed method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art trajectory-conditioned video generation baselines (Tora, DragAnything, MotionCtrl, IRASim) on the Bridge dataset across both visual metrics (FVD, PSNR, SSIM, VBench) and trajectory-following accuracy.

Downstream robotics validation: The authors validate the utility of the generated videos for robot learning by training an inverse dynamics model and demonstrating superior execution success rates on RLBench and SIMPLER compared to OpenVLA, Tora, and TesserAct.

Thorough ablations: The ablation studies effectively dissect the individual components, including causal latent propagation, mask- vs. point-based representations, separate vs. collaborative trajectories, trajectory perturbations, and prompt noise.
Clear presentation and reproducible pipeline: The paper is well-organized, with well-designed diagrams and an extensive appendix detailing data curation and user annotation.
weaknesses: Reliance on temporal phase boundaries: At test time, the model requires defining the interaction phase boundaries (start and end frames F1, F2). While the authors present a Gradio demo for human annotation, this requirement adds manual overhead or depends on heuristic motion thresholds, limiting fully automated, large-scale data synthesis.

Restriction to 2D trajectory space: Manipulation tasks inherently depend on 3D spatial reasoning (depth, 6-DoF gripper orientation, contact forces). Operating purely in 2D image coordinates can lead to depth ambiguities and physically inconsistent grasps or placements under varied camera viewpoints.

Details of downstream policy execution: The pipeline extracts action sequences from generated videos and deploys them onto simulated robots, suggesting open-loop execution. It is unclear whether actions are executed strictly open-loop or if a closed-loop policy is trained on synthetic rollouts, which is critical for understanding robustness to compounding errors.

Automatic segmentation reliability: As noted in Table R11, off-the-shelf grounding models (Grounded-SAM) achieve low success rates (14–21% in multi-object scenes), underscoring a significant dependency on manual masking in non-trivial environments.
